entry.title: Is your website caught up in October’s security problems?

link.title: Is your website caught up in October’s security problems?

entry.content:
I worked on PHP and LAMP sites years ago, so I’ve seen both sides of PHP. It’s a big part of why so many small businesses could get online cheaply. It’s also why one flaw can reach so many of them at once.

October brought one of those flaws, plus two certificate problems. There have been plenty of headlines and not much plain advice for the people who actually own these websites. So here’s what I’d check if I ran a small business or a community group in Australia or New Zealand.

Most of you will find you’re fine. It takes about ten minutes, and you don’t need to be technical. Facts are as at 25 October 2026.

Check 1: who issued your website’s certificate?

Your certificate is what puts the padlock in a visitor’s browser. Two certificate problems came up this month, and one has a deadline of 27 October.

To see who issued yours, go to ssllabs.com/ssltest (free, run by the security company Qualys), tick “Do not show the results on the boards”, and enter your web address. After a minute or two (if you see a list of servers, click any one), look at the certificate’s “Issuer” and “Revocation status” lines. “Good (not revoked)” is what you want to see.

If you see What it means What to do
Starfield or Go Daddy, and the status says revoked GoDaddy revoked about 380,000 certificates this month because the paperwork behind them didn’t match GoDaddy’s own published rules. Nothing was hacked, but a revoked certificate no longer works properly Log in to GoDaddy and reissue and install the certificate, or ask whoever set up your site
Starfield or Go Daddy, not revoked Not affected. GoDaddy has finished revoking every certificate caught up in this Nothing to do
emSign, or EM DV, EM OV or EM EV That certificate company’s signing keys were weak enough for anyone to recover. Chrome has already blocked the worst of them, and on 27 October (US time, so 27 or 28 October here) it stops trusting the whole emSign ECC Root CA - G3 family. The company has since said it is leaving the website certificate business Get a replacement from a different certificate company now, before 27 October
Anything else Neither problem applies to you Nothing to do

When I checked on 25 October, neither Australia’s ACSC (Australian Cyber Security Centre) nor New Zealand’s NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre) had published anything on either certificate problem. Both have published on PHP.

Check 2: does your website run on PHP?

On 21 October PHP got an urgent fix for two flaws that let someone take over a website without a password. Attackers started trying them on 17 October, before the fix was out. As at 25 October, no successful break-ins had been confirmed, and Australia’s ACSC said it knew of none here, but this is the one to act on.

Your site almost certainly runs PHP if it’s built with WordPress (WooCommerce shops included), Joomla, Drupal or Magento, or if your hosting account has a cPanel or Plesk control panel. If it’s on Squarespace, Wix or Shopify, the platform runs the servers, so this one is their job.

If your site does run PHP, you almost certainly can’t fix it yourself. Your host can, and most will already be on it. What you want is a clear answer in writing. This is the email I’d send:

Subject: PHP security update for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Hi, my website [your web address] is hosted with you. PHP released urgent security fixes on 21 October 2026 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Could you please confirm in writing:

  1. Which PHP version runs my website, and does it include the fixes for these two flaws?
  2. On what date was the update installed and PHP restarted?
  3. If my website runs an older PHP version (8.1 or earlier), what is your plan for it?
  4. Did you check my website for signs of a break-in before you installed the fix?

Keep the reply, and don’t judge it by the version number alone. Hosts often fix older-looking versions without changing the number. Ubuntu’s fixed build, for example, still reads 8.3.6, which looks a long way behind PHP’s own fixed 8.3.36. If your control panel shows PHP information, the build date is a better sign: Hostinger tells customers that a build dated 21 October 2026 or later has the fix, and VentraIP also points to the build date.

If your plan is a “VPS” or “unmanaged”, your host probably expects you, or whoever set it up, to do the update. GoDaddy, Hostinger, SiteHost and 1st Domains all say so for those plans.

If you use WordPress, one more check. The company behind the UpdraftPlus backup plugin was broken into over the weekend of 17 and 18 October, and attackers used its remote-management connections to add admin accounts and plugins to some customers’ sites. If you connected your site to UpdraftCentral, its cloud dashboard: log in to WordPress directly, update UpdraftPlus to 1.26.13 (free) or 2.26.13 (Premium) or later, remove any administrator or plugin you don’t recognise, and change your passwords.

The bigger question: do you still need this website?

This is the part I’d spend the most time on. Every website has to be kept up to date, forever. If yours isn’t earning its keep, this is a good moment to decide.

Three questions: how many real people visited in the last three months (ignore huge “hits” numbers, which are mostly bots); did any enquiries, bookings or sales come through it; and does it do something nothing else does, like an online shop, bookings or member logins?

Your answers Option
Real visitors, and it takes orders, bookings or logins Keep it. Get the host’s written answer above and keep plugins up to date
Real visitors, but it’s just information about you Simplify it. Turn it into plain pages with no PHP behind them, which several services host for little or nothing, or move it to a site builder that does the updating for you
Hardly anyone visits, but you want a record Archive it. Save a copy, take it offline, and leave one page with your contact details
Nobody visits and it does nothing for you Retire it, after the checks below

Before you cancel or move anything:

  1. Check where your email lives. Many small businesses’ email runs on the same hosting as the website. Ask your host whether yours does before you cancel anything.
  2. Keep your domain name on auto-renew, even if the website goes. A lapsed domain can be bought by someone else and used to pretend to be you.
  3. Forms and bookings need a new home if the site becomes plain pages.
  4. Save a copy first. Your host can make a full backup.

Other things this month

  • Windows: make sure the October 2026 update is installed (Settings, then Windows Update, then Update history). Attackers are already using one of the flaws it fixes.
  • Your backups: if a company backs up your business, ask whether their service runs on AhsayCBS and whether they’ve installed the October hotfix.
  • If an IT company looks after your network: ask whether they use Fortinet, Palo Alto, BeyondTrust or Ivanti products for you, and whether those have this month’s updates.

If you think you’ve already been hacked

Call before you delete anything. In Australia: the Australian Cyber Security Hotline, 1300 CYBER1 (1300 292 371), or IDCARE’s free small-business helpline, 1800 595 170. In New Zealand: the NCSC on 0800 114 115 (free, 7am to 7pm, Monday to Friday), or report online at ncsc.govt.nz/report.
entry.summary: Ten minutes of checks for Australian and New Zealand small businesses: who issued your certificate, whether your site runs PHP, what to ask your host, and whether you still need the site at all.

entry.title: Separating human, agent and CI credentials as a solo operator

link.title: Separating human, agent and CI credentials as a solo operator

entry.content:
One login, three actors: separating human, agent and CI credentials when AI agents do the work

I run ImpactEng on my own, and a lot of the hands-on work now goes through AI coding agents. From mid-September I started bringing the pieces together. Most already followed the same conventions. They just didn't share one way in. In October I set out to make that one governed path for deploying infrastructure to every provider I use. One rule sits at the centre: I approve every production deploy.

This post follows an earlier piece, Where AI Agents Break Your CI/CD Pipeline, which looked at the pipeline itself. This one covers the credentials behind it.

Where it started

The path covers more ground than a one-person business might suggest. Deploys go to AWS, Cloudflare, GitHub Pages and Google Apps Script. Code lives on GitHub and on a self-hosted Git forge, secrets sit in a password manager, and CI (continuous integration) does the deploying. Several AI coding agents do much of the preparation, Claude Code among them. I wanted one way in, so that at any time I could say what was deployed where, and by whom.

The path as it stands now.

The approval rule matters most to me. An agent can prepare a change; only I let it reach production.

Why it changed

Then I looked at what the one GitHub login on my machine could do. Everything: push to any repository and start runs. And every agent session used it, because the agents ran as me.

So in principle an agent could edit the deploy workflow, remove the check that enforced my approval, and start a run. My approval gate meant poop while the agents held the trigger.

The first fix: split the login

It looked like an easy fix. Give each actor its own root of trust: me, CI and the agents. My own GitHub login has always lived in my password manager; now the command-line token goes through it too, so using it needs my fingerprint (and a little patience). The agents got a narrow token of their own. CI was planned around short-lived federated credentials through OIDC (OpenID Connect) wherever a provider supports them, so that no long-lived Cloud key has to sit in a repository.

The problem was real, and splitting the login was the right call. The way I did it caused most of what came next. Good intentions, road to hell, you know the rest.

What it broke

I removed access without first listing what it was used for. Within days the agents could no longer read CI results or open pull requests. My own login lost access I still need now and then, such as organisation settings. And my tests checked each token's settings. None of them ran a real task, such as an agent opening a pull request.

One gap I knew of and left open. A push over SSH (Secure Shell) doesn't care about token permissions, and I had written that down at the start. It stayed a note until an agent session pushed a branch as me. 🤦

Doing it again, from an inventory

Second time round, I started with what we actually used. I went through what the old login had been used for, by me and by the agents, and listed every workflow that touched GitHub: reading CI, opening a pull request, creating a repository, merging, settings. For each one I wrote down how it worked before, after, and how it should work. That table became my test plan.

I also added a guard at the git level so that an agent session doesn't push as me by accident. Its first version rewrote push addresses, and a git setting I hadn't accounted for got round it. The second, which replaced it, refuses the push itself.

GitHub helped with one of the losses. In October it added a narrow Repository creation permission, so I can create repositories again without the wider permission, and the agents still can't. I covered that step in a short LinkedIn post.

One thing I'd recommend: commits made in an agent session are now authored and signed as the agents, under their own name and signing key, but they keep my GitHub noreply email address. The history shows the work as the agents', and by GitHub's rule it should still count on my contribution graph, because GitHub credits a commit by its email address, and the noreply address counts (GitHub Docs).

What changed my mind

There was still a gap GitHub couldn't see. The agents' token sat on my own account, so as far as GitHub could tell, everything done with it was done by me. Merging a pull request needed no permission beyond what an agent already held to push a branch. So GitHub couldn't tell an agent's merge from mine. "Agents never merge" only held because the agents behaved.

Turns out this is a known mistake. AWS lists it for IAM (Identity and Access Management) in its guidance for agentic AI: reusing human user credentials or roles for agent authentication, which makes it "impossible to distinguish agent actions from human actions in audit logs" (AWS Well-Architected, Agentic AI Lens).

The pattern I found in vendor docs and in other solo operators' write-ups has three actors and three credentials. The agent works under its own identity and can at most push a branch. The human approves and merges as a different identity. CI holds the deploy credential, through short-lived federation where the provider offers it.

Where it landed, for now

By that pattern, the agent needs its own identity. Its commits already carried one, but GitHub's own logs still saw only me. I also started on the shape other solo operators describe: a free machine account as a collaborator with write access, and a main-branch rule requiring a review the agents can't give. Then the merge decision would sit with GitHub.

Setting it up, I had to change the plan twice. The token I meant to give the machine account couldn't be made: a fine-grained token on that account could reach only repositories it owned, and it owns none. And on GitHub's free plans, rulesets are available only on public repositories (GitHub Docs), so on a private repository the review rule isn't enforced. There, any credential that can push a branch can also merge it. Both facts were cheap to check, and I should have checked them before deciding.

So I went with the simplest option, one GitHub doesn't have to enforce: the agents hold no write credential on GitHub, and their old token is revoked. They prepare branches under their own identity, and I push them and merge the pull requests. Read-only access will give them back most of what they lost, since most of what they did on GitHub was reading. If pushing by hand becomes a chore, there is a researched way to split the permissions across two GitHub Apps, so that the one able to open a pull request can't merge it. I haven't tested it yet.

Two things I'm still working out. The first is an operating system boundary for agent sessions, a microVM (a lightweight virtual machine) or a second user account. The second is providers without OIDC. Cloudflare's guide for deploying from CI still asks for an API token stored as a secret (Cloudflare Docs), so for providers like that the plan is to keep the deploy token behind the same approval gate, out of the agents' reach.

Over to you

How have you separated human, agent and CI credentials? I'm most interested in solo operators and small teams, and in anyone doing it across several providers at once, where each one has its own idea of identity.

If you've solved this, or you're partway through, I'd like to hear how. Get in touch or book a time to talk.
entry.summary: How I split one GitHub login into separate credentials for me, my AI coding agents and CI, what the first attempt broke, and where it landed.

entry.title: A shared AI platform for APRA-regulated organisations

link.title: A shared AI platform for APRA-regulated organisations

entry.content:
A team asks to put an AI assistant in the contact centre. It sounds like another pilot. In an organisation regulated by APRA (the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority) it isn't: under CPS 230, APRA's operational risk standard, it can make your shared AI platform part of a critical operation.

Over two weeks I wrote 14 LinkedIn posts on designing one AI platform for every team in a regulated organisation, and getting teams to use it. This is the whole path in one place, from the first request to the twentieth app, including what I tested along the way. Each section links the posts it comes from. Facts about Amazon Web Services (AWS) are as at October 2026.

  1. A request arrives
    Is it part of a critical operation? Then it may not be a pilot.
  2. The door
    Six questions decide what gets built before a team gets access.
  3. Where data goes
    Set per type of data. Tested: the hole in my own residency policy.
  4. One way in
    No other path to a model, no emergency bypass. Fail closed.
  5. Who spent it
    Tested: billing names the team, but only by the day. Meter every request.
  6. The twentieth app
    Scale by triggers, not the calendar. Watch the queue before the route-around.

1. Two filters

My first instinct was a catalogue: every capability a shared AI platform could need. It told me nothing about what to build first, or what's expensive to get wrong. So I put two filters on it. Does most of the usage need this on day one? And if we get it wrong, how much do we rip up later? High on either, and it gets decided now.

The second filter earns its place. On usage alone you'd cut the audit trail and per-team telemetry, because hardly any traffic depends on them early. But you can't go back and collect what you never logged. Of 33 candidate capabilities, 18 are in from the start, nine are decided now and built later, and six are parked, each with a named trigger that brings it back. (Post 1)

2. Not every request is a pilot

CPS 230 lists customer enquiries as a critical operation unless you can justify otherwise, and the systems that support it come along too. So a summariser for an internal team is one thing; a staff assistant in the contact centre is another. When one of those comes through, the platform picks up tolerance levels for disruption approved by the Board, a 24-hour clock to tell APRA when a disruption goes beyond them, and a way for the business to keep going without the AI. None of it is hard if you've seen it coming. (Post 4)

3. Decide the shape now, build it later

Early in the design, I made up seven that might one day use the platform: a squad prototyping an idea, a staff assistant, back-office processing, a customer-facing assistant, decision support, an agent that calls other systems, and developers' coding tools. Each was a test: for every decision, would this have to change to serve one of the later ones? The customer-facing assistant bit. It needs to know which customer is behind a request, even if only by a pseudonym, and adding that later would change how every app calls the platform. So the field went in on day one. (Post 3)

The simplest of the nine "decide now, build later" items is a cost centre on every request, even when nobody is charging anyone yet. Charging back can wait. The field goes in now, because adding it later means changing every app and tool already calling the platform. (Post 2)

4. The questions at the door

Six questions decide what gets built for a team before it gets access:

  1. Does it support a critical operation? Then it needs a fallback without the AI (section 6).
  2. Does it make or feed decisions about people? Then the human check has to be real, and from 10 December 2026, under the Australian Privacy Principles (APP 1.7 to 1.9), if those decisions could significantly affect someone, your privacy policy has to say so.
  3. Is it public-facing? Then it comes through its own backend, with stricter guardrails and limits per customer.
  4. Does it search company knowledge? Then the platform has to know who's asking, so search returns only what they may see.
  5. Will it call tools or take actions? Then it needs limits on steps, tokens and which tools.
  6. Has your risk team cleared its data for offshore processing? The default answer is no.

The first team to say yes to any of these builds that piece for everyone after them. Every team also names who owns it, how risky it is, how someone could challenge it, and when it gets looked at again. (Post 13)

5. Where the data may go

Global cross-Region inference on Amazon Bedrock, AWS's managed model service, costs roughly 10 per cent less than keeping it in Australia. Whether you take it depends on what you're sending. Bedrock's Australian inference profile keeps processing in Sydney and Melbourne. If a use case supports a critical operation, sending it offshore is material offshoring, and APRA wants notice beforehand; the Privacy Act keeps you accountable for personal information you send overseas. So I set it per type of data, not once for the platform: synthetic or public data can go global and take the saving, anything personal or critical stays here until risk says otherwise. And if a check spots personal information in a prompt, it can only move the request somewhere stricter. (Post 5)

The home Region matters too. Bedrock Guardrails' newer Standard tier runs through a cross-Region profile. From Sydney, the Australian profile keeps the checks in Sydney. From Melbourne, the only profile on offer is Asia Pacific, so the checks can go to several countries; Melbourne's other option is the Classic tier, which keeps the checks in Melbourne but has less robust protection, and a customer-facing app is where you want the stronger one. I'd pick Sydney. (Post 9)

What I tested: the hole in my own residency policy. On the AWS account where I test the design, I deny Bedrock model calls outside Australia. The policy named Bedrock's two invoke permissions. Then I found Bedrock has a second endpoint, bedrock-mantle, with its own permission, which a deny on those, or on bedrock:*, doesn't cover. The AWS IAM (Identity and Access Management) policy simulator confirmed it: bedrock:InvokeModel came back explicitDeny, bedrock-mantle:CreateInference allowed. Bedrock Guardrails don't run on that endpoint and model invocation logging doesn't capture it. CloudTrail records those calls only as data events, which are off by default. So a call through it gets past the residency policy, the guardrails and, by default, the logs. The fix was one extra statement denying bedrock-mantle:*. (Post 8)

6. One way in, and no bypass

Who, apart from the platform's gateway, can call a model? If the answer is "a few teams, for now", every control on the gateway is optional for them. (Post 7)

A related request sounds reasonable: an emergency bypass for when the platform is down. The answer is no. The bypass is the path with no redaction and none of the platform's audit trail, used at exactly the moment nobody is watching closely. So the platform fails closed, with a clear error the app can handle, and the fallback lives with the app: a way to run the business process without the AI. Where the AI supports a critical operation, APRA expects that fallback to be credible. It has to meet a minimum standard I'm still defining, so it's shown to work. On the platform side, the answer is redundancy that keeps every control, including a second route to models that has been tested. (Post 11)

7. Knowing who spent it

What I tested: can AWS billing name the team? Claude on Bedrock is billed through AWS Marketplace, and AWS attributes cost by the day, not by the request. The documentation didn't say whether your own tags reach Claude's lines on the bill, so I tagged an application profile and a role as if they belonged to a team, made a handful of calls, and waited for the cost report. It cost less than a cent. The tags did reach the Claude charges, next to the role that made the calls. (Post 10)

That's good enough for a monthly showback (reporting spend by team, without charging it back), and no use for a quota that has to act in seconds. So the platform meters every request itself, keyed by the app and cost centre that made it, and the bill is what you reconcile against at the end of the month.

8. The twentieth app on a shared AI platform

The twentieth app is the real test. I'd scale by triggers rather than by calendar: prove the path on made-up data, then first production (often a staff assistant), then many kinds of app at once, then isolate the group that needs its own limits. None of those triggers can fire unless each app has been measured from day one: tokens, throttling, latency, and how long onboarding takes. (Post 12)

Adoption fails in one of two ways. The platform team becomes the queue every team waits in, or teams tire of waiting and route around it, straight to a model with their own credentials. You see the queue first, in two numbers: how long onboarding takes and how many teams are waiting. My starting points are more than ten business days, or more than five teams; your own onboarding times will tell you the real ones. Cross either, and add these one at a time, moving on only if the last one didn't fix it: a paved road (a client library and working examples), then self-service onboarding, then a platform team that only looks at the exceptions. (Post 14)

9. What I'd do the same way

Most of this came from asking the questions. The second endpoint only turned up while I was working out how to make the platform the only way to reach a model. When the documentation didn't say whether a batch job would take the Australian profile, I ran one. It was accepted and completed, though I've only tried one Claude model. Cheap decisions get the simple option; expensive ones get tested before I trust them. (Post 6)

Talk to me

If you're working through any of this, whether it's the six questions, your residency policy or the onboarding queue, I'd like to hear where you've got to.

Book a free 30-minute call

entry.title: Your platform team is about to inherit the AI problem. Most aren’t ready.

link.title: Your platform team is about to inherit the AI problem. Most aren’t ready.

entry.content:
Gartner forecast in 2024 that 80% of large software engineering organisations would have dedicated platform teams by 2026, up from 45% in 2022. The 2025 DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) report puts current adoption at nearly 90%. The teams exist. What they're being asked to absorb on top of that is a different question.

AI workloads.

Not as a side project. Not as a prototype sitting on someone's laptop or a sandpit cloud account. As a core platform capability, governed, deployed, and maintained with the same rigour as your CI/CD pipeline or your container orchestration layer. Platform Engineering and AI are fusing in 2026, and most teams are unprepared for what that actually requires.

Why platform teams are getting the AI problem

It's not random. There's a logic to why AI is landing in the platform team's lap.

Enterprise AI deployment has a governance problem. Accelirate's analysis estimates that governance gaps, not model failures, will drive 40% of enterprise AI project failures by late 2026. A Cloud Security Alliance survey of 285 IT and security professionals, run in late 2025, adds weight to that: only 21% of organisations keep a real-time inventory of their AI agents, fewer than a third (28%) can reliably trace an agent's actions back to a person or system, and 44% use or plan to use static API keys to authenticate them. These look like AI problems on the surface. Underneath, they're platform engineering problems: identity, observability, governance. They have to be solved on the platform, not in each AI application.

Weave Intelligence's State of AI in Platform Engineering report (2025) finds three-quarters of organisations are already hosting or preparing to host AI workloads on their platforms. Whether the platform is ready is the harder question.

For most organisations, the Internal Developer Platform (IDP) is the natural place to absorb AI workloads. It already owns the guardrails, the identity model, the deployment gates, and the observability contract. That's exactly what AI workloads need and almost never have when they're built somewhere else.

Two caveats. Some organisations are standing up purpose-built "Platforms for AI" alongside their IDP, separating GPU orchestration and model lifecycle from general engineering. And in most large enterprises I've worked in, the "IDP" is closer to a mesh of overlapping platforms with different conventions per team than a coherent single system. Identity, observability, and governance still belong with platform engineering. They can't be enforced consistently when the platform itself isn't.

The problem is that most platform teams were built to solve CI/CD, containerisation, and developer experience. They were not built to handle inference workloads, agentic orchestration, multi-model cost optimisation, or the governance implications of autonomous systems taking actions in production.

I wrote in March about the trap of mandating platform adoption. The same readiness gap shows up here from the other direction: AI work is now being mandated onto platforms whether they're built for it or not.

What the dual mandate actually requires

Platform Engineering maturity in 2026 is being measured against what The New Stack recently called a dual mandate: augmenting the platform with AI capabilities while building the platform infrastructure that governs AI workloads at scale.

Both sides of that mandate are hard.

Augmenting the platform with AI means integrating AI coding assistants, predictive automation in CI/CD, and AI-assisted observability. DORA's 2025 research puts AI adoption across software engineering at 90% and finds that AI is an amplifier: it magnifies strength in high-performing teams and dysfunction in struggling ones. The same pattern shows up in the pipeline. Bolting a coding assistant onto a CI workflow is not the same as redesigning the pipeline to be AI-aware: context-managed, hallucination-resistant, and able to gate on confidence rather than just test pass rates.

Governing AI workloads on the platform is the harder side. It means the platform team needs to own:

Circuit breakers for agent pipelines that auto-trip on consecutive failures before errors cascade. Confidence gating logic that routes agent outputs to human review below a threshold rather than auto-executing. Audit trails that track not just what an agent did, but what it believed when it acted, and how those beliefs have changed over time. FinOps (cloud financial management) controls specific to AI: model selection cost gates, token budgeting, and the infrastructure to make smaller, cheaper models default unless larger-model performance is explicitly required.

None of this is in the platform engineering playbook as it was written three years ago.

Where Australian platform teams are starting from

The Australian context adds a layer of complexity that global trend reports skip.

Data residency requirements under the Australian Privacy Act and the government's cloud security policies constrain which AI services can be used for which workloads. You can't just route everything through a US-based inference endpoint. Platform teams in regulated sectors such as financial services, government, and healthcare need to bake data residency into their AI deployment model at the infrastructure level, not as a policy afterthought.

The skills gap is also acute. AI-capable platform engineers are in short supply globally and more so here. The AWS AI/ML Scholars program, which opened its 2026 cohort to as many as 100,000 free learners worldwide, is a signal that the hyperscalers recognise the gap. But training 100,000 people in foundational generative AI skills does not produce platform engineers who can design and operate agentic governance infrastructure. That's a different thing.

A pattern I see: the platform team that handles 40+ deploys a day across environments without breaking a sweat, then stalls when asked who owns the identity for the AI agent their data science team just stood up. The instinct is to treat AI workloads like any other application workload: build it, containerise it, ship it. That instinct fails when the workload can take autonomous actions, when its outputs are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and when its failure modes cascade differently from anything the on-call runbook was written to handle.

Practical takeaway

If you lead a platform team and AI workloads are already in your backlog or about to be, three things are worth addressing before you take on more:

Define your agent identity model. Every AI agent running on your platform should have a unique, auditable identity. Not a shared service account. Not a static API key. A real identity with scoped permissions and rotation policies. This is the single highest-impact governance improvement and the most commonly skipped.

Build confidence gating into your deployment pipeline. AI agent outputs should have a confidence threshold that determines whether they auto-execute, get flagged for human review, or trigger an escalation. This belongs in the platform, not in the individual application.

Extend your observability contract to cover AI-specific signals. Token consumption, model latency, confidence score distribution, correction rates, and escalation frequency are the metrics that will tell you whether your AI workloads are healthy. Your existing dashboards don't surface these.

The platform team that builds the safe foundation for AI workloads in their organisation becomes the team that owns AI adoption at scale. That's a significant opportunity. But it requires acknowledging that the platform engineering playbook needs updating before the AI problem arrives and not after.

Ready to talk?

If you're working through this and want a second perspective, get in touch. I've been on the platform team side of this for a decade and now work the AI and platform intersection through ImpactEng. Strategy, hands-on, or both, whichever is most useful.

Book a free 30-minute call
entry.summary: AI workloads are landing on platform teams that weren't built for them. Here's what the dual mandate requires, and where Australian teams stand.

entry.title: Your AI coding session is a finite resource. Manage it like one.

link.title: Your AI coding session is a finite resource. Manage it like one.

entry.content:
You are forty minutes into a refactor. The model has read the relevant files, understands the architecture, and is tracking changes across five modules. Then something shifts. It starts repeating suggestions you already rejected. It re-reads files it loaded twenty minutes ago. The responses get vaguer. The session is rotting, and you have no useful signal about it.

I would restart at this point, paste in a quick summary of where I am, and lose twenty to thirty minutes rebuilding context. It might happen three or four times a day, and I would accept it as the cost of using these tools. It does not have to work this way.

A note on scope: when I first outlined this, I was thinking about the broader problem of dependency on a single session, single tool, or provider. That is a real problem but too large for one post. This one focuses on AI session management specifically. The deeper idea is picking up exactly where you left off in a completely different tool (and provider), not just a fresh session of the same one. That comes later. The protocol I describe here is designed with that portability in mind.

The mental model you actually need

Every AI coding session operates across three resource layers, and none of them refill mid-session.

The context window is working memory: what the model can see right now. Every file you attach, every response the model generates, every tool call and its output burns from this budget. When it fills, quality degrades before it hits a hard wall. Models do not announce this politely. They just get worse.

Tokens are fuel. They are consumed on both sides of every exchange: your input, the model's output, tool invocations, file loads. Most tools give you some visibility into this, though the granularity varies considerably across products.

Subscription capacity is your weekly tank. Hit the cap and you are out until it resets, regardless of which tool you are using or how important the deadline is.

None of this is hidden information. The tools expose it. The problem is that most developers never look until something breaks.

What visibility actually looks like across tools

The tools vary considerably on how much they surface these constraints during a session.

Claude Code has a /context command that breaks down current token usage by category: system prompt, tool definitions, memory files, conversation history. It also auto-compacts when the context window approaches its limit, summarising conversation history to reclaim space. Persistent instructions in a CLAUDE.md file survive across sessions, so you are not re-explaining project conventions every time you start fresh.

Cline shows token counts and cost per request in real time, and tracks cumulative spend for the entire task. It also creates checkpoints after tool calls, so you can restore the session to an earlier state if the model heads in the wrong direction. That combination of cost visibility and rollback capability makes it the most transparent option for sustained, expensive workloads.

Kiro and Windsurf both surface context usage in their UIs, with varying levels of detail depending on which mode you are using. Windsurf's Cascade mode is particularly good at loading only what is relevant rather than forcing you to manage file attachment manually.

The honest summary: all of them have improved significantly, but none give you a unified view across sessions or providers. If you are switching tools mid-project, which is increasingly common as teams standardise on different IDEs, you are doing that accounting yourself.

When to act: the thresholds worth tracking

You need three trigger points, and acting on any one of them is enough.

The first is context fill. When you are at 50 to 60 per cent capacity, act. Below that threshold it is premature. Above it, most tools will auto-summarise in ways you did not choose, and you lose fidelity on what gets kept. Check the context command or UI indicator; do not wait for degradation signals in the responses.

The second is token volume. Around 15,000 to 25,000 tokens consumed in a session is when quality starts to drift in most models. This is independent of context fill percentage because it correlates with how much reasoning the model has had to do, not just how full the window is. Tool-heavy agentic sessions, like the kind that interact directly with your CI/CD pipeline, burn through this budget faster than you expect.

The third is time. Thirty to forty-five minutes of active, tool-heavy use is a reasonable default if you are not watching the other two. Set a timer for the first session or two until checking context becomes habitual.

The practical action is simple: check context, then run a canned prompt. Something like: "Summarise the current state of this work in 400 tokens or fewer: what has been done, what files were changed, and what comes next." Save that output. You will need it.

The handoff protocol

Whether you are approaching a limit, switching providers, or ending the day, the handoff process is the same and takes under two minutes.

Ask the model to generate a handoff.md: current architecture decisions, open questions, exact files to reopen, and a brief summary of the conversation so far. Git commit everything, including the handoff file. In the next session (whether that is a fresh Claude Code session, Cline, Kiro, or Windsurf), attach handoff.md and the three to five most relevant files. Skip the full conversation history.

This works across every tool I listed. The reason it works is that it does not depend on any tool's internal state. It is just a structured text file that any model, in any harness, can read and orient from. That is the point: the protocol is tool-agnostic by design, which means it also covers the case where you are moving to a completely different product mid-project.

The sessions where I rebuild from a handoff.md consistently feel indistinguishable from the ones where the context never lapsed. The sessions where I do not have one feel like starting cold, even when they are not.

The shift that actually matters

The tools will keep improving. Context windows are getting larger. Visibility is getting better. Some tools now handle compaction well enough that you will not notice the boundary at all.

But the mental model is the durable thing. Treat every session as temporary from the first message. Build checkpoints before you need them. Keep a handoff.md in your project root and update it when triggers fire, not when you are desperate.

Three things worth doing this week:

  • Add a handoff.md to your current project root. Generate a first version now, before a session dies and forces you to.
  • Check your primary tool's context indicator on your next session. Note what 50 per cent capacity feels like before quality drops.
  • Write your state summary prompt once and save it somewhere you can paste it quickly. You will use it more than you expect.

The developers who do this consistently waste almost no time on resets. The ones who do not rebuild context from memory every time they hit a wall. That gap compounds across a working week faster than most people realise until they measure it.

If you are running AI-assisted development at any volume, session management is not optional. It is just infrastructure you have not set up yet.

entry.title: The Platform Engineering trap: why mandating your platform makes things worse

link.title: The Platform Engineering trap: why mandating your platform makes things worse

entry.content:
The DORA research programme has now tracked platform engineering across multiple years. The pattern is consistent: good platforms, freely adopted, improve performance. Mandated platforms reduce it. In 2024, across 39,000 practitioners, teams required to exclusively use their internal developer platform saw throughput fall by 8% and change stability fall by 14%.

The 2025 report did not reverse that finding. It added a sharper edge: when platforms are poorly designed, AI adoption does not offset the damage. It amplifies it.

This is the trap a significant number of Australian engineering teams are building their way into right now.

What Platform Engineering is supposed to do

Platform Engineering emerged as an answer to a real problem. As organisations scaled, the DevOps ideal of "you build it, you run it" started to break under its own weight. Product teams were expected to manage Kubernetes, observability, security, secret management, cost tagging, and compliance tooling, on top of shipping features. The cognitive load became the bottleneck.

Platform Engineering resolves this by building internal infrastructure as a product. A dedicated platform team creates curated, maintained pathways ("golden paths") that developers use because they genuinely reduce friction, not because they are required to. The goal is to take decisions off product teams' plates, not to recentralise control under a new name.

That is the theory. The practice has drifted considerably from it in a large number of organisations. And in Australia, the problem is concrete: 532 banking outages totalling nearly 1,500 hours in 30 months (RBA, 2024), a single CrowdStrike software update in July 2024 that simultaneously brought down banks, telcos, and airlines, and 69% of tech leaders reporting weekly disruptions from foundational IT flaws, twelve points above the global average (KPMG, 2024). The platform layer, where it exists at all, is not solid.

Where it goes wrong

The mandate problem is the most data-supported trap, but it is not the only one.

The portal trap came first. Between 2022 and 2024, many organisations treated Backstage, the CNCF developer portal framework, as synonymous with "building a platform." Teams spent 12 to 18 months implementing portals. The portal surfaces what the platform offers. But if the underlying orchestration layer, deployment abstractions, and service ownership model are not there, the portal is a catalogue with empty shelves. Developers open it once and stop coming back. The agentic systems now running in your CI/CD pipelines expose this gap quickly. They assume coherent, queryable infrastructure and find a patchwork instead.

The measurement trap follows. According to the State of Platform Engineering 2024 report, 45% of platform teams do not measure success at all. A further 26% cannot determine whether their metrics improved after implementing their platform. When adoption stalls and the platform team cannot demonstrate why the investment is worth continuing, the response is often to mandate adoption, which is precisely how you arrive at the DORA outcome.

The mandate trap is the terminal stage of this sequence. The platform team, under pressure to show adoption numbers, requires product teams to use the platform. Product teams, who were not involved in the platform's design and are now blocked on existing workflows, experience it as a constraint rather than a capability. Throughput falls. Confidence in the initiative falls. Budget follows shortly after.

The DORA finding is sometimes misread as "mandates are always wrong." They are not. I have been on the platform team side of this: hands-on pairing with leads and seniors, competing visions surfaced and addressed, a clear technical case for the new direction. The teams eventually understood. We still needed a hard block to get there. What DORA is capturing is mandates that substitute for that groundwork, not mandates that follow it.

Why this hits Australian teams harder

There is no Australian-specific platform engineering adoption survey. No ANZ equivalent of the DORA report, no local breakdown in the platformengineering.org State of Platform Engineering study. Australian engineering leaders are navigating this without local benchmarks, which makes it harder to know whether your experience of these traps is common or exceptional.

The talent picture makes the organisational dynamics particularly difficult. Platform Engineering is a senior discipline: 47% of platform engineers globally have more than eleven years of experience (State of Platform Engineering 2024, platformengineering.org). Australian tech attrition sits at 19.2%, above the 17% global average (Ravio, 2025). Organisations are competing for a small pool of senior people who leave at above-average rates. You cannot hire your way to platform maturity. And when the person who built the platform leaves, the initiative often leaves with them.

ThoughtWorks Australia has written specifically about the political blockers in Australian-context organisations: the silo effect (platforms do not cross departmental lines, adding complexity rather than removing it), the cost-centre perception (platform teams funded as operational overhead rather than value drivers), and the single-champion dependency (the initiative stalls when the champion departs). All three are structural, not technical. Tooling does not fix them.

The one clear Australian counterexample is Commonwealth Bank. CBA was processing 3,000 production changes per month at the point they committed to platform engineering as a product discipline (Atlassian, 2024). By AWS re:Invent 2024, their CTO reported doubling that in a single year, while reducing incident volume and duration (AWS re:Invent ARC206; iTnews, 2024). The critical detail is how: their engineering platform team operates with a defined north star, tracks developer experience metrics, and measures adoption of internal tooling. It was built around what engineers actually needed, not presented as infrastructure they were required to use.

What gets out of the trap

The organisations with working platform engineering practices share a few consistent patterns.

They start with developer pain, not tooling selection. They survey developers, talk to product teams, and find the three things that slow developers down most. The platform addresses those things first. The result is that developers want to use it, which generates adoption data that justifies continued investment without needing a mandate.

They measure adoption, not existence. Platform uptime is the wrong metric. I know because I have tracked it. Uptime tells you the lights are on. It says nothing about whether anyone is using the room. The right ones are: what percentage of new services use the standard pipeline? What is the time-to-deploy for a new service started from scratch? How many support requests does the platform team handle for self-service capabilities? These metrics distinguish a platform people use from a platform people have been told to use.

They protect developer autonomy. Golden paths are suggestions backed by investment, not mandates. The paved road is more convenient than going off-road: better documentation, faster setup, proven security controls. Adoption can happen through pull, not push. Teams that can demonstrate this to executives do not necessarily need to mandate anything. The adoption data speaks for itself.

And they get executive sponsorship that is not personality-dependent. The CBA example took years and sustained commitment at the leadership level. Organisations that treat platform engineering as a single champion's initiative will cycle through the trap repeatedly.

I work with Australian engineering teams on platform engineering assessments, tooling decisions, and organisational design. Platform maturity matters for AI too: you cannot reliably run agentic systems on a fragile foundation. If you want to know where your delivery toolchain stands, my Software Delivery Assessment covers that directly. For the organisational side, see the work beyond the assessments.

entry.summary: Most platform engineering initiatives focus on tooling and adoption targets. Two years of DORA data shows mandated adoption actively reduces delivery performance, and AI makes it worse. Here is what that means for Australian engineering leaders.

entry.title: So I failed the AWS SA Pro exam by 17 points. Then I built SonicCert Coach.

link.title: So I failed the AWS SA Pro exam by 17 points. Then I built SonicCert Coach.

entry.content:
I failed the AWS Solutions Architect Professional exam by 17 points. Not 50 points. Not "I didn't study." Seventeen points, after a few months of preparation.

The root cause wasn't effort. The problem was where that effort went. I kept going deep on the domains I found interesting and avoided drilling the ones which mattered more. The exam does not care what you find interesting. It weights domains. I didn't respect those weights. So I ate dirt.

A few months later, I went through a run of certification exams across AWS, Azure, GCP, and Oracle, eight or nine over about two to three months. Again, I failed the OCI Data Science Professional exam too, by a small margin. Same mistake, different exam. WTH!

A note on why I bother

I get it. Some engineers think certs are noise. I don't fully disagree. But for me, right now, they serve a real purpose. They give structure to a learning path and a clear target when I'm running a business. And they provide an external credibility signal for clients who don't know me yet. I'll take that tool.

The problem isn't certs. The problem was how I was studying for them. Going deep on interesting topics feels productive. It isn't, when the exam has a blueprint and you're ignoring it.

Why a hackathon

When this Amazon Nova AI Hackathon came up, I signed up for a few reasons. I wanted to build something. I've spent a long time in roles where I admired the people who shipped things, and I'm at a point in my career where I want to be one of those people, not just the person who knows how to run the infrastructure underneath it.

I also wanted to stretch deliberately. Cloud, Infrastructure, Developer tooling come naturally to me. That's not enough for me anymore. Python proficiency, product thinking, solid software engineering chops, building for an end user: these are skills I'm consciously developing. A hackathon with a real deadline felt like the right constraint to force it.

And I had a specific problem to solve.

The Nova Sonic problem

The original vision for SonicCert Coach was voice-first. Real-time bidirectional audio: speak to it like a tutor, have it quiz you back, evaluate your answer out loud, and push you toward your weak spots. The name comes from Amazon Nova Sonic, AWS's new audio model.

I spent the first couple of days trying to make that work. The experimental AWS SDK has a method called invoke_model_with_bidirectional_stream. It hangs. Indefinitely. I tried multiple SDK versions and reproduced it on official AWS sample code. My conclusion: boto3 doesn't support bidirectional streaming yet. It is a genuine bug in early-access infrastructure, or at least that's what I found. I'd be happy to be corrected.

At some point you have to decide: keep fighting or ship something that works. I pivoted the architecture entirely. The name stayed.

What I built

SonicCert Coach is a multi-agent AI tutoring system on Amazon Bedrock. Nova Pro runs as the orchestrator: multi-turn reasoning, tool-use routing, session memory. Three specialist agents run on Nova Lite, which is fast and cheap for focused single-shot tasks:

  • Question Generator: creates domain-targeted questions weighted to the real exam blueprint
  • Answer Evaluator: scores your response and explains what was right and wrong
  • Study Advisor: tracks your accuracy by domain and recommends what to drill next

Grading logic and session memory are plain Python. Deterministic problems don't need a language model. Bedrock's tool-use pattern handles routing: the orchestrator decides which specialist to call, passes the context, gets the result back. It never tries to do everything itself.

One orchestrator. Three specialists. Two Python tools. Every component has a clear job.

If you're new to AI, my primer on AI fundamentals for DevOps and Cloud engineers covers the building blocks.

What using it looks like

It's a CLI. You pick a target exam (say, AIF-C01 AWS AI Practitioner), set your proficiency level, and choose batch or interactive mode. The system pulls your prior session data, targets your weakest domains first aligned to the exam's actual weightings, quizzes you, evaluates your answers with explanation, and gives you a domain-by-domain breakdown at the end.

The weak command cuts to it: here is what you are getting wrong, and here is how that maps to exam weightings. Not what you find interesting. What the exam tests.

That's the thing I needed and didn't have when I sat that exam.

Where this goes

I plan to keep working on it. It's not where it needs to be yet. The voice layer is still on the list: I haven't given up on Nova Sonic, I've just parked it until the SDK is actually usable. Session persistence works but it's JSON-based and won't scale if this ever becomes something more than a personal tool. There are product decisions I haven't made yet.

But it already does the thing I built it to do. It has helped me see where my knowledge has actual gaps. That's worth something on its own.

No promises on timeline. But I'm not putting it down.

If you want to see the hackathon submission, it's at devpost.com/software/update_later.

I created the project intending to rename it before submission. I did everything except that. Support confirmed it can't be changed. Fitting, really.

Building something on Bedrock?

Whether you're exploring multi-agent patterns for a personal project or assessing what agentic AI means for your team, let's talk it through.

entry.title: The sovereignty gap: why cheap AI comes with real risks for Australia

link.title: The sovereignty gap: why cheap AI comes with real risks for Australia

entry.content:
I've been full-time in the AI space since last year, working with Australian tech teams. We've all seen the toggle: "Do not use my data for training." We click it, breathe a sigh of relief, and keep building.

But here's the uncomfortable truth: every major model provider still captures and retains request/response data for legal, safety, and compliance reasons. Anonymised datasets can still be re-identified through modern AI mosaic attacks. And in the process of learning patterns of malicious behaviour, edge-case IP and sensitive ideas can quietly migrate into internal models.

The data we're actually sharing

On the ground, I'm seeing teams continue to paste information into these tools without really thinking through what tiers of data are being processed and logged. It sits dormant until, one day, it either gets deliberately used or mistakenly surfaces.

The financial math that moves entire economies is at play here: massive capital flowing into a handful of frontier players, uncertainty about who the winners and losers will be, questions around their ethics, and how much real control nations and societies actually retain while trying to keep an open marketplace alive.

Add in the job shifts already happening and the way other critical research domains are quietly starved of funding, and the stakes feel existential.

The real trade-off

It feels uncomfortably familiar. The same dynamic we saw with earlier platforms where the service was free and the real product was the user. Only now the stakes are higher: our ideas, our research, our public-service data (health, aged care, education, pensions, disability support), and ultimately our national capability.

The trade-off is real. Frontier models through cloud APIs are dramatically cheaper and more capable than self-hosting or local rigs for the vast majority of use cases. Market forces and network effects are already steering us toward a handful of dominant providers. That's great for speed and iteration. It's risky for long-term control.

Especially when we reach AGI and the shortest pathway to prosperity for one business or nation might simply be: look at all the existing data and amplify your wealth and power, so we can do good for humanity.

What Australia is actually doing

Australia is not standing still. The National AI Plan (December 2025) and the APS AI Plan, with its GovAI sovereign platform, show genuine intent: keeping public-sector data inside Australian infrastructure, establishing the AI Safety Institute (now operational), and focusing on practical productivity gains across health, education, aged care and more.

These are meaningful steps. The government is investing in sovereign capability, not just talking about it.

Yet for national security especially, the question is sharper: do we really want to depend on providers like Palantir or Anduril for the capabilities that protect us? Most Aussies, easy-going and with the right heart, would rather spend that money looking after our people. But the world is not a super-safe space.

You will need capabilities. Period. Or we put our next generations at the mercy of others and their shifting notions of righteousness.

The speed with which friends can become adversaries (US tariffs being a recent reminder) should give every policymaker pause.

What engineers are actually implementing

From the trenches, here's what practical controls look like today:

  • Data tier classification: Teams are starting to classify data before it touches an LLM. Public, internal, confidential, restricted. Different tiers get different treatment.
  • Request logging and audit trails: Every API call logged with metadata. Who sent what, when, to which provider. Retention policies that actually get enforced.
  • Local model deployment for sensitive workloads: Running Llama or Mistral on-premises for anything that touches customer PII or proprietary IP. Yes, it's slower. Yes, it's more expensive. But you control the data.
  • API gateway controls: Rate limiting, content filtering, and automated redaction before requests leave the network perimeter.
  • Vendor contract scrutiny: Actually reading the data processing agreements. Understanding where data is stored, who has access, and what happens when you terminate the contract.

These aren't theoretical. These are the controls that separate teams who are thinking about sovereignty from teams who are just hoping for the best.

The conversation we need

This isn't about rejecting powerful AI. It's about ensuring we use it on terms that reflect Australian values, starting at home, while still contributing responsibly to global progress.

We need genuine, cross-domain perspectives:

  • AI engineers building production systems: What practical controls are you actually implementing today around data tiers and logging?
  • Frontier thinkers and educators: How do we make sovereignty, accessibility, and open-market innovation compatible at scale?
  • Global safety leaders and academics: Where should the balance between open innovation and protective guardrails sit, especially as AGI pathways emerge?
  • National-policy, privacy, and security experts: What regulatory or infrastructure moves would actually move the needle for public services and national security without slowing us down?

Where this leaves us

The window for shaping this is narrowing. Every team that pastes sensitive data into a frontier model without thinking through the implications is making a choice, whether they realise it or not.

The National AI Plan is a start. The AI Safety Institute is operational. GovAI is being built. But the real work happens at the team level, in the decisions engineers make every day about which model to use, which data to send, and which controls to implement.

entry.title: Where AI agents break your CI/CD pipeline

link.title: Where AI agents break your CI/CD pipeline

entry.content:
Everyone is talking about AI agents in CI/CD. GitHub shipped Agentic Workflows. AWS announced frontier agents at re:Invent 2025. Deloitte's latest State of AI report says 74% of companies plan to use agentic AI at least moderately within two years.

Here is the part nobody is talking about: most CI/CD pipelines were designed for a human clicking "merge" a few times a day. Not for an autonomous agent generating hundreds of commits per hour.

I spent the better part of a decade running CI/CD platforms at scale, including a migration from Bamboo to GitLab serving 650+ users across hundreds of microservices. That experience taught me exactly where pipelines buckle under pressure. Agents apply that same pressure, only faster and less predictably.

Five ways your pipeline breaks

1. Pipeline triggers assume human cadence

Most pipeline configurations assume a human-paced workflow. A developer pushes a branch, opens a merge request, waits for review. The system handles a handful of concurrent runs per project.

AI agents do not work that way. A coding agent can generate pull requests every few minutes. Multiply that by the number of repositories it has access to and you get hundreds of pipeline triggers in a burst. Runner pools exhaust. Queue depths spike. Jobs that used to take eight minutes now wait forty because every runner is occupied by agent-generated work.

The fix is not just adding more runners. You need concurrency controls at the agent level: rate limits, priority queues that distinguish human-initiated from agent-initiated runs, and circuit breakers that pause agent triggers when pipeline load crosses a threshold.

2. Artifact storage was not built for this volume

Every pipeline run generates artifacts: container images, test reports, compiled binaries, dependency caches. When humans drive the pipeline, the volume is manageable. When agents drive it, the numbers change fast.

An agent that opens 50 pull requests a day across a monorepo generates 50 container images, 50 test report archives, and 50 sets of build logs. Multiply that across a dozen repositories and your artifact registry is growing by gigabytes per day. Retention policies that assumed weekly cleanup cycles now need daily or hourly cleanup. Storage costs that were a line item become a budget conversation.

The deeper problem is versioning. Agents generate code variations at a speed that makes tracking "which version came from which agent run" genuinely difficult. Without explicit agent run IDs in your artifact metadata, debugging a production issue becomes archaeology.

3. Approval gates agents cannot pass

Approval gates exist for a reason. They enforce human judgement at critical points: before merging to main, before deploying to production, before modifying infrastructure. The problem is that these gates were designed as blockers. They assume a human will be available to review and click "approve" within a reasonable timeframe.

Agents generate changes at machine speed. If your pipeline has three manual approval stages, your agent-generated work piles up behind each one. The result is either a backlog that defeats the purpose of agent-generated speed, or teams start rubber-stamping approvals to clear the queue, which defeats the purpose of the gates entirely.

The industry is converging on what some call "safe output" patterns. Instead of giving agents direct commit access, agents produce proposed diffs. Instead of triggering deployments, agents generate action plans that a policy engine validates. The agent recommends; the system enforces. It is a fundamentally different approval model from "wait for a human to click a button."

4. Secrets management was not designed for machine delegation

Your pipeline secrets, API keys, service account tokens, deployment credentials, were provisioned for specific services and specific humans. AI agents need access to the same secrets but through a completely different trust model.

When a human runs a pipeline, the identity chain is clear: user authenticates, triggers pipeline, pipeline assumes a service role. When an agent triggers a pipeline, the identity chain gets murkier. Which agent? Acting on whose behalf? With what scope? For how long?

Most secrets managers do not have a concept of "agent identity" as distinct from "service identity." The result is either agents running with overly broad credentials (a security incident waiting to happen) or teams manually creating per-agent service accounts (which does not scale). This is not a hypothetical problem. Deloitte's 2026 report found that only 21% of companies have a mature governance model for autonomous agents, and their governance section explicitly calls out the need to "define which decisions agents can make independently versus which require human approval."

5. Observability has blind spots for agent behaviour

Your monitoring stack tracks pipeline success rates, build duration, test pass rates, and deployment frequency. These metrics assume deterministic, repeatable workflows. Agent-driven pipelines are neither.

An agent might produce a passing build that introduces a subtle regression because the test suite was not designed to catch the kind of changes agents make. Or an agent might trigger a cascade of infrastructure changes across multiple environments simultaneously, something your alerting rules never anticipated because no human would do that.

The gap is not just metrics. It is traceability. When a production incident traces back to an agent-generated change, you need to reconstruct what the agent was trying to do, what context it had, what alternatives it considered. Current pipeline observability tools do not capture any of this.

As a recent New Stack infrastructure guide put it: "Most failures in early agentic systems stem not from model quality but from missing isolation, poor observability, and unbounded cost growth." The model is not the problem. Your pipeline is.

The industry is responding, but most enterprises are not

The vendors are moving. GitHub's Agentic Workflows embed agent runners directly into the CI/CD execution model. AWS shipped dedicated DevOps agents that maintain state, log actions, and operate within policy guardrails. These are not proof-of-concept demos. They are infrastructure-grade primitives designed for agent workloads.

But the vendors being ready does not mean enterprises are ready. Deloitte surveyed 3,235 business and IT leaders globally and found that technology infrastructure preparedness is actually declining: 43% rate themselves highly prepared, down four percentage points from the previous year. Strategy confidence is rising. Operational readiness is falling. That gap is exactly where AI agent failures will happen.

The Australian picture is sharper. Nutanix's Enterprise Cloud Index found 90% of Australian respondents say AI is accelerating their container adoption. That is encouraging. But adopting containers and having a CI/CD pipeline that can handle autonomous agent workloads are very different things. You can be running everything on EKS and still have a GitLab pipeline that breaks the moment an agent starts committing code at machine speed.

Deloitte's report puts it bluntly: 84% of companies have not redesigned jobs or the nature of work around AI capabilities. If you have not rethought the work, you definitely have not rethought the pipelines that support the work.

What your pipeline actually needs

If you are planning to introduce AI agents anywhere near your CI/CD system, here is what to address first.

  • Isolation per agent run: Every agent-triggered pipeline run should execute in an isolated, reproducible environment. No shared state between runs. No assumptions about what the previous run left behind. This is the same principle as hermetic builds, applied to agent workloads.
  • Policy gates instead of human gates: Replace manual approval steps with policy-as-code validation. Define what an agent is allowed to change (file paths, resource types, blast radius) and enforce it automatically. Reserve human approval for changes that exceed the policy boundary, not every change.
  • Agent-aware observability: Tag every pipeline run with agent identity, intent, and context. Log not just what happened but why the agent thought it should happen. Build dashboards that track agent-specific metrics: change velocity, rollback frequency, policy violations, cost per agent run.
  • Concurrency and cost controls: Set hard limits on concurrent agent-triggered runs per repository and per agent. Implement cost ceilings per agent per billing period. These are not optional. Without them, a misconfigured agent can burn through your CI/CD budget in hours.
  • Secrets with agent-scoped identity: Provision short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials for each agent session. Use your Cloud provider's identity federation (AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, GCP Workload Identity) to bind agent identity to pipeline credentials. Audit every secret access against agent identity, not just service identity.

None of this requires ripping out your existing pipeline. It requires extending it with agent-aware controls. If you are already running a mature CI/CD platform, the foundations are there. The work is in adapting them for a new class of consumer that is faster, less predictable, and does not read your runbooks.

My Software Delivery Assessment maps how you build, test and ship, which is where agent workloads land first. Pipeline readiness for agent workloads is where I see the biggest gaps between what organisations think they are ready for and what they actually are.

The bottom line

AI agents in CI/CD are not hype. They are coming, and for some organisations they are already here. But the infrastructure most teams are running was not built for them.

The companies that will adopt agentic workflows successfully are not the ones with the most advanced AI models. They are the ones with CI/CD pipelines that can handle non-deterministic, high-concurrency, machine-speed workloads without falling over. That is an infrastructure problem, not an AI problem.
